title: Why Full-Duplex Speech Models Collapse in Long Conversations

paper.title: Why Full-Duplex Speech Models Collapse in Long Conversations
paper.abstract:
Abstract Full-duplex speech models listen and speak at the same time, which makes
them promising for natural, open-ended conversation. But can they sustain
a coherent conversation for tens of minutes? Because they generate a token every frame, even while listening, they
exhaust their context windows within minutes. Yet existing benchmarks
evaluate only single turns or a few conversational rounds, too short to
expose the long-horizon problem. We introduce the Full-Duplex
Long-Horizon Benchmark (FD-LHB), which tests five recent full-duplex models on long replayed
conversations and in live conversation with an LLM partner. Every evaluated model eventually either degrades or exhausts its context. Models that keep the full history often degrade before their context runs out, while sliding-window models still fall into repetition , silence , and gibberish . For sliding-window models, we identify two contributing mechanisms. Gibberish and silence are linked to Initialization-Anchor Eviction,
where the sliding window discards the first KV entry. Repetition is also reinforced by the model’s own recent outputs. Guided by this diagnosis, we apply two simple fixes:
Initialization-Anchor Pinning (IAP) keeps that first entry, and
Duplex Repetition Penalty (DRP) discourages echoing while guarding
against prolonged silence. Together, they support the diagnosis and, without retraining, substantially reduce conversational collapse in replays of up to an hour while running in real time.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: 0 min — coherent “Hi, my name’s Alex. I’m in the Seattle area. Where are you?” 6 min — repetition “… you go back to your normal life , you go back to your normal life , and then you go back to your normal life …” 9–10 min — silence (no lexical output) 13 min — gibberish “core offensive of the core the good blue of the event seven…” Figure 1: Example of long-conversation collapse. It shows progression of coherent speech, repetition, silence, and gibberish, with timestamps aligned to the timeline in Figure 2a. Human conversation can continue for tens of minutes or longer, as speakers move between long turns, silence, interruptions, backchannels (e.g., “uh-huh” or “yeah”), and overlapping speech ( Levinson and Torreira, 2015 ) . Full-duplex speech models ( Défossez et al., 2024 ; Roy et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) aim to support this form of interaction by listening and speaking concurrently. Maintaining this behavior over long conversations remains difficult because, unlike text LLMs or half-duplex systems, full-duplex models continuously generate tokens frame by frame, even while listening. This rapidly fills the context with silence and recurring backchannels, while each generated output also becomes part of the next input and can influence later generation. Despite these challenges, long-horizon behavior in full-duplex models remains poorly understood. Existing full-duplex benchmarks ( Lin et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2026b ; Lin et al., 2026a ; Peng et al., 2025 ; Arora et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2026 ) evaluate capabilities such as turn-taking, interruption handling, pauses, backchanneling, and overlapping speech, within a single turn or a few conversational rounds, not over many minutes. Existing models manage conversation history in one of two ways. Growing-context models ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) keep the full interaction, so their context grows until it reaches a context limit. Sliding-window models ( Défossez et al., 2024 ; Roy et al., 2026 ) keep only the most recent frames, discarding the oldest as new ones arrive, so they can run indefinitely with fixed-size cache. Whether either design is sufficient for long-form full-duplex interaction, and how the models fail when it is not, has not been systematically investigated. Figure 2: How three models degrade over a long conversation. Top: repetition and gibberish rate; middle: occurrence of each failure mode; bottom: output words per minute. Sliding-window models (a) PersonaPlex and (b) Moshi exhibit an initial period of coherent speech, followed by silence and eventual gibberish, with repetition emerging at different times. The growing-context model (c) BayLing-Duplex develops gibberish and silence before reaching its context limit. To investigate this problem, we introduce the Full-Duplex Long-Horizon Benchmark (FD-LHB) , a benchmark designed specifically to evaluate full-duplex models over extended interaction. FD-LHB combines controlled replay of CANDOR conversations ( Reece et al., 2023 ) with adaptive interaction against an LLM-based spoken partner. Using FD-LHB, we find that every evaluated model eventually either degrades, through repetition, silence, or gibberish ( Fig. 1 ), or exhausts its context: sliding-window models collapse even though their memory never runs out ( Fig. 2 a,b), and growing-context models can collapse before reaching their context limit ( Fig. 2 c). We then ask why these collapses occur, focusing on the two sliding-window models, and identify two contributing mechanisms ( Sec. 4 ). Silence and gibberish are linked to Initialization-Anchor Eviction : the sliding window eventually discards the first KV entry computed without prior cached context. We hypothesize that this dependence reflects a mismatch between empty-cache training and continual inference. We also identify Self-Reinforcing Repetition : a word the model has recently said becomes more likely to be said again. Finally, these mechanisms motivate two simple fixes that need no retraining. Initialization-Anchor Pinning (IAP) keeps the first KV entry in the cache while the rest of the window slides as usual, and Duplex Repetition Penalty (DRP) discourages recently used words without making the model less likely to speak. Together, they substantially reduce repetition, silence, and gibberish in both sliding-window models. In addition, the combined method still runs in real time and is faster than a StreamingLLM-style baseline ( Xiao et al., 2024b ) while matching its cache stability. We do not claim that they solve long-horizon full-duplex modeling; rather, our results show that simple fixes targeting the two identified causes prevent much of the collapse. Our contributions are as follows: • FD-LHB: benchmark for long-horizon full-duplex interaction. FD-LHB measures when and how conversational failures emerge through two tracks: 40 controlled replays evaluated up to 60 minutes (FD-LHB-CANDOR) and 40 adaptive sessions up to 20 minutes (FD-LHB-LLM). • Systematic characterization and diagnosis of collapse. Across five recent full-duplex models using sliding-window or growing-context, we characterize the onset and progression of three failure modes: repetition, prolonged silence, and gibberish. Experiments on two sliding-window models identify Initialization-Anchor Eviction and Self-Reinforcing Repetition as mechanisms underlying the collapse. • Validation through training-free interventions. Simple, targeted fixes reduce gibberish from 100% to 0%. Repetition falls from 65% to 0% in Moshi and 90% to 2.5% in PersonaPlex; prolonged silence falls from 100% to 7.5% and 85% to 47.5%, respectively. These interventions require no retraining and can be incorporated into compatible baselines at inference time.

sections.heading: 2.1 Full-Duplex Speech Generation and Streaming Interaction
sections.text: Models such as Moshi ( Défossez et al., 2024 ) , PersonaPlex ( Roy et al., 2026 ) , Raon-SpeechChat ( Kim et al., 2026 ) , BayLing-Duplex ( Fang et al., 2026 ) , and Lychee-FD ( Liu et al., 2026 ) support low-latency full-duplex interaction. Existing benchmarks ( Lin et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2026b ; Lin et al., 2026a ; Peng et al., 2025 ; Arora et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Ray et al., 2026 ) evaluate turn-taking, overlap, interruption handling, multi-round quality, and task completion, but do not examine their stability over extended conversations. We address this gap by evaluating repetition, silence, and gibberish during continuous generation lasting tens of minutes.

sections.heading: 2.2 Long-Horizon Stability and KV-Cache Management
sections.text: Autoregressive generation can suffer from degeneration in text ( Holtzman et al., 2019 ) , video ( Ge et al., 2022 ) , and speech ( Song et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) . Scheduled Sampling ( Bengio et al., 2015 ) and Professor Forcing ( Lamb et al., 2016 ) address the mismatch between training and generation through modified training procedures. We instead investigate instability during continual full-duplex inference, where generated outputs can reinforce later repetition ( Xu et al., 2022 ; Zhu et al., 2023 ) . DRP targets this feedback by modifying token selection without retraining. Beyond repetition, continual inference raises the question of how conversation history should be retained. Under a fixed memory budget, StreamingLLM ( Xiao et al., 2024b ) preserves initial attention sinks together with recent tokens, as do LM-Infinite ( Han et al., 2024 ) and InfLLM ( Xiao et al., 2024a ) ; H2O ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) retains tokens with high accumulated attention; and SnapKV ( Li et al., 2024 ) selects prompt positions using attention patterns from an observation window. Building on these studies, we examine the role of the first KV entry in the long-horizon stability of full-duplex speech models. StreamingLLM is the closest to IAP because it also preserves entries from the beginning of the sequence. In Moshi and PersonaPlex, the first KV entry alone prevents gibberish in all tested runs, whereas the tested later entries do not do so consistently ( Sec. 4.1.2 ). We hypothesize that this dependence reflects initialization-anchor eviction: training chunks always begin with this entry, but long inference evicts it ( Sec. 4.1 ). IAP keeps only this entry and updates only its position index, which is cheaper than re-indexing the whole cache as StreamingLLM does ( Sec. 6.4 ).

sections.heading: 3.1 Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: Existing benchmarks do not test whether these models remain stable over sustained interactions lasting tens of minutes. To address this gap, we introduce the Full-Duplex Long-Horizon Benchmark (FD-LHB). FD-LHB has two complementary tracks: controlled replay ( FD-LHB-CANDOR ) and adaptive interaction ( FD-LHB-LLM ). Replay (FD-LHB-CANDOR) gives every model the same recorded human speech, enabling controlled comparison, but it is non-interactive: the input doesn’t respond to the model’s output. Adaptive (FD-LHB-LLM), by contrast, is interactive, with an LLM partner whose synthesized speech reacts to the model’s behavior like a real conversation, but this means the input differs across runs, making controlled comparison harder. Because each track compensates for the other’s weakness, the two are complementary.

sections.heading: FD-LHB-CANDOR.
sections.text: FD-LHB-CANDOR is built from CANDOR ( Reece et al., 2023 ) , a corpus of long, natural human conversations. We remove the first three turns from each conversation to exclude greetings and initial silence, rank the conversations by their remaining duration, and select the longest 40. The resulting streams have minimum, mean, and maximum durations of 55.5, 67.4, and 92.6 minutes, respectively. We evaluate each replay for up to 60 minutes, or until the available conversation ends. For each conversation, we select the speaker channel containing more speech and use it as the fixed audio input to the evaluated model. Thus, although the original CANDOR recordings are interactive human conversations, FD-LHB-CANDOR replays the same fixed input to every model, enabling controlled comparison.

sections.heading: FD-LHB-LLM.
sections.text: To complement the non-interactive fixed replay of FD-LHB-CANDOR, FD-LHB-LLM evaluates the model in a closed-loop conversation with an LLM-based spoken partner whose responses adapt to the evaluated model’s output. At each turn, Gemini-2.5-Flash ( Comanici et al., 2025 ) generates the partner’s next text response from the recent dialogue history, and a local facebook/mms-tts-eng VITS model ( Pratap et al., 2023 ) converts it to 16-kHz speech for the evaluated model. The evaluated model’s response is then returned to Gemini, which generates the next partner turn. Each session begins with one of ten everyday-life topics, such as hobbies, travel, family, or work, and the partner responds adaptively to the evaluated model rather than following a fixed script. We run 40 sessions per dialogue model, each for up to 20 minutes or until the model reaches its context capacity.

sections.heading: 3.2 Failure Modes and Onset Metrics
sections.text: As shown in Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 , we observe three main forms of long-horizon collapse: repetition , silence , and gibberish . To measure when each form first appears, we define its onset time . Repetition is evaluated over 32-word windows, while silence and gibberish are evaluated in one-minute bins. For each form, the onset is the start of the first window or bin that meets its criterion.

sections.heading: Repetition.
sections.text: We measure repetition with word-level Seq-Rep-4 ( Xu et al., 2022 ) , which captures repeated four-word patterns in the model’s recent output. We use this metric because it detects recurring phrase-level patterns. We compute it over 32-word windows and define a window as repetitive when Seq-Rep-4 ≥ 0.30 \geq 0.30 ; examples around this threshold are shown in Table 3 . The repetition onset is the start of the first of two consecutive repetitive windows, so a single repeated phrase is not counted.

sections.heading: Silence.
sections.text: We measure silence using the number of spoken words in each bin. A bin is considered silent when it contains fewer than three words. To exclude short conversational pauses, we define prolonged-silence onset as the first bin of two consecutive silent bins.

sections.heading: Gibberish.
sections.text: We characterize gibberish using two measures: a Gemini-2.5-Flash judge and predictive entropy, computed from the model’s distribution over its next text token. Gemini classifies each one-minute speaking bin as either gibberish or non-gibberish, while predictive entropy measures the model’s uncertainty. We evaluate bins containing at least three words and define the gibberish onset as the first bin classified as gibberish by Gemini. A blinded listening study with eight raters shows that the judge never calls normal speech gibberish but sometimes misses real gibberish ( Sec. A.3 ), so the reported gibberish rates may be slightly lower than the true rates. We do not use external-LM perplexity; Sec. A.5 explains why. Figure 3: Initialization-Anchor Eviction. When training starts each chunk from an empty cache, every chunk begins with a fresh initialization anchor. In sliding-window inference, the cache is never reset, so the initial anchor is eventually evicted.

sections.heading: 4 Diagnosing Long-Conversation Collapse
sections.text: Based on FD-LHB ( Sec. 3 ), we next investigate the mechanisms behind the three forms of collapse observed in Fig. 2 : repetition, silence, and gibberish.

sections.heading: 4.1 Initialization-Anchor Eviction
sections.text: The similar timing of silence and gibberish in Moshi ( Défossez et al., 2024 ) and PersonaPlex ( Roy et al., 2026 ) shown in Fig. 2 motivates us to examine their shared cache-management strategy. Both models use a sliding window that discards the oldest cached entries as new ones arrive. As shown in Fig. 3 , training splits each sample into chunks that start from an empty cache, so every chunk begins with an initialization anchor : the first KV entry, computed without any earlier cached state. We confirmed this setup in the official Moshi fine-tuning code; whether pretraining and PersonaPlex training follow it is not public ( Sec. B.1 ). At inference, however, the cache is never reset. Once it is full, the oldest entries are evicted, starting with the initialization anchor. Training therefore always contains an anchor, whereas long inference eventually does not, creating a training–inference mismatch. We hypothesize that this initialization-anchor eviction causes the collapse and test this hypothesis in Secs. 4.1.1 and 4.1.2 .

sections.heading: 4.1.1 Collapse Timing Follows Cache Turnover
sections.text: Figure 4: Silence and gibberish track cache turnover. Collapse onset time versus attention-window length W W . (a) Conversational input. (b) Silence-only input. Silence and gibberish begin later as W W grows, roughly in proportion to W W . Based on the initialization-anchor eviction hypothesis ( Sec. 4.1 ), we vary the attention-window length W W and measure when each type of collapse begins ( Fig. 4 ). Results from Moshi and PersonaPlex are combined. Fig. 4 a shows the results with conversational audio input. Silence onset grows at ( 1.63 ± 0.49 ) ​ W (1.63{\pm}0.49)W and gibberish onset at ( 2.70 ± 0.20 ) ​ W (2.70{\pm}0.20)W . Repetition, in contrast, varies widely across runs and shows no clear relation to W W . To separate cache turnover from conversational content, Fig. 4 b repeats the sweep with silence-only input. Gibberish still appears and grows at ( 2.54 ± 0.19 ) ​ W (2.54{\pm}0.19)W , whereas repetition does not start later as W W grows. These results show that silence and gibberish onsets scale roughly with W W , with gibberish following this pattern even in the absence of conversational content, linking these failures to cache turnover, while repetition shows no consistent relationship. We investigate repetition further in Sec. 4.2 .

sections.heading: 4.1.2 The first KV entry is sufficient
sections.text: Based on the initialization-anchor eviction hypothesis ( Sec. 4.1 ), we investigate which cache entry and how many entries must be retained to prevent gibberish. In both experiments below, we measure the percentage of runs that do not produce gibberish over time ( Fig. 5 ). Results from Moshi and PersonaPlex are combined. In Fig. 5 a, we keep exactly one early entry in the cache and vary only which one it is: the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 9th, or 17th entry, or the entry at L / 4 L/4 , L / 2 L/2 , or 3 ​ L / 4 3L/4 , where L L is the window length. Only the entry itself changes; its place in the cache and its position index stay the same. Surprisingly, only the first entry prevents gibberish in all runs; every other choice fails in at least one run. In Fig. 5 b, we keep the first P P consecutive entries, with P ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 , 64 , 128 } P\in\{0,1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128\} . With P = 0 P{=}0 , every run reaches gibberish. With any P ≥ 1 P{\geq}1 , no run does, and the curves overlap exactly. Together, these results show that the first entry alone prevents gibberish in all tested runs, and keeping more initial entries gives no further improvement. Figure 6: Recent outputs reinforce repetition. (a) Top 10 repeated words during repetition periods; orange marks backchannels. (b) Share of each PersonaPlex run’s dominant word around repetition onset; seven diagnostic runs without a sustained onset are excluded. (c) Share of purple in the 20 s after inserting it d d times.

sections.heading: 4.2 Recent Outputs Reinforce Repetition
sections.text: We next examine whether repetition in full-duplex speech is driven by self-reinforcement. In text generation, repeated content in the context makes the same content more likely, so a loop can reinforce itself ( Xu et al., 2022 ; Zhu et al., 2023 ) . Based on this, we hypothesize that recent outputs similarly reinforce repetition in full-duplex speech, and test this hypothesis in Fig. 6 . First, the most repeated words during repetition periods are short, frequent words such as of , then , and you , and backchannels such as yeah and okay ( Fig. 6 a). Second, for each PersonaPlex run we select the word that dominates during repetition periods and track how frequently it occurs. It starts rising before onset and keeps rising afterward ( Fig. 6 b). This suggests that a repetition loop does not appear suddenly, but grows from a word the model has already been saying. Third, we insert purple , a word absent from the previous context, and count how often the model repeats it over the next 20 s. Recurrence increases with more insertions in both models, most strongly in PersonaPlex ( Fig. 6 c). Together, these results show that recent exposure makes a word recur.

sections.heading: 5 Testing the Diagnosis with Training-Free Interventions
sections.text: The diagnosis yields two testable predictions: retaining the initialization anchor should reduce failures associated with cache eviction, and limiting reinforcement from recent words should reduce repetition. We test these predictions with Initialization-Anchor Pinning (IAP) and Duplex Repetition Penalty (DRP), respectively. Both are training-free methods that operate at inference time and can be applied to existing models.

sections.heading: 5.1 Initialization-Anchor Pinning (IAP)
sections.text: Sec. 4.1.2 showed that keeping the first KV entry is enough to prevent gibberish, while keeping more initial entries adds nothing. IAP therefore keeps this initialization anchor instead of letting the sliding window evict it. Until the cache is full, nothing changes. Once it is full, the model normally drops the oldest entry each time a new one arrives. IAP does the same, except that it never drops the anchor: when a new entry arrives, it removes the oldest entry after the anchor instead. This is done in every layer. As in StreamingLLM ( Xiao et al., 2024b ) , the anchor’s position index stays next to the rest of the window so that position indices remain continuous. StreamingLLM, however, re-indexes the entire cache as the window slides. IAP instead simply increases the anchor’s index by one each time the window slides. Only this single entry changes, which keeps IAP cheap ( Sec. 6.4 ).

sections.heading: 5.2 Duplex Repetition Penalty (DRP)
sections.text: DRP reduces repeated words without letting the model fall silent instead. It changes only the assistant’s text-token logits; the audio streams are unchanged. DRP penalizes any word that appeared in the model’s last N = 512 N{=}512 lexical tokens, using the standard repetition penalty of CTRL ( Keskar et al., 2019 ) : a positive logit is divided by ρ \rho and a negative one is multiplied by it. A word is penalized based only on whether it appeared recently, not on how often. PAD and EPAD , which the model uses for listening and turn-taking ( Roy et al., 2026 ; Défossez et al., 2024 ) , are excluded from this penalty. Penalizing words lowers their total probability and makes PAD and EPAD relatively more likely. To undo this, we raise all word logits by the same amount, so that the total probability of words stays the same as before the penalty. This removes the relative boost that the penalty gives to PAD and EPAD. With this penalty alone, repetition decreases, but PAD can still dominate for long periods, leaving the model silent. To address this, when the model has been silent for a long time and the user is quiet, we gradually lower the PAD logit. We do not force any token; the model still samples its next token as usual ( Sec. C.2 ).

sections.heading: 6.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: We evaluate five full-duplex models using two context-management strategies: sliding-window and growing-context. Moshi ( Défossez et al., 2024 ) and PersonaPlex ( Roy et al., 2026 ) are sliding-window models with a 3,000-frame window at 12.5 Hz, so their window first fills after four minutes. Raon-SpeechChat ( Kim et al., 2026 ) , BayLing-Duplex ( Fang et al., 2026 ) , and Lychee-FD ( Liu et al., 2026 ) are growing-context models that run until their context is full, after about 5, 17.5, and 10.9 minutes, respectively. Reaching context capacity ends the run; this limits sustained operation but is not counted as a collapse event. In Fig. 7 , such runs are right-censored: they count as failure-free until they end, and the curves are estimated with the Kaplan–Meier method ( Kaplan and Meier, 1958 ) . We apply IAP+DRP to the two sliding-window models, since anchor eviction occurs only when a sliding window discards old entries. Generation settings for each model are given in Table 9 .

sections.heading: 6.2 Main Results
sections.text: Fig. 7 shows how long each system stays free of each collapse on FD-LHB-CANDOR (top) and FD-LHB-LLM (bottom); “Ours” denotes IAP+DRP. Observation lengths differ across models, so we compare methods within each model rather than across models. All percentages below are computed over 40 runs per system.

sections.heading: Every baseline fails, in one of two ways.
sections.text: On FD-LHB-CANDOR ( Fig. 7 , top), growing-context models run out of context or collapse first: Raon-SpeechChat reaches capacity after about five minutes, BayLing-Duplex shows repetition, silence, and gibberish in 55%, 100%, and 90% of runs within 17.5 minutes, and Lychee-FD shows repetition and gibberish in 37.5% and 30% within 10.9 minutes. Sliding-window models never exhaust their context but still collapse: over 60 minutes, Moshi and PersonaPlex show the three failures in 65/100/100% and 90/85/100% of runs. FD-LHB-LLM shows the same pattern ( Fig. 7 , bottom). Thus, none of the evaluated models sustains stable conversation over tens of minutes, regardless of how it manages its context. Figure 7: Repetition, silence, and gibberish across replay and adaptive interaction. Top: FD-LHB-CANDOR; bottom: FD-LHB-LLM. Curves show the percentage of runs remaining free of repetition (a, d), prolonged silence (b, e), or gibberish (c, f) over time; higher is better. For growing-context models, a plus marks where the model reaches its context capacity. IAP+DRP largely suppresses repetition and gibberish in both models and reduces prolonged silence.

sections.heading: IAP+DRP reduces collapse.
sections.text: We apply IAP+DRP to the two sliding-window models. On FD-LHB-CANDOR, the repetition, silence, and gibberish rates drop to 0%, 7.5%, and 0% for Moshi, and 2.5%, 47.5%, and 0% for PersonaPlex. The PersonaPlex+Ours silence in Fig. 7 b is mostly temporary: 94.7% of the affected runs resume speaking within a minute after the two-minute silence. On FD-LHB-LLM, where the partner responds to the model, the baselines also fail frequently, most often through gibberish (97.5–100% of sessions) and prolonged silence (70–87.5%). With IAP+DRP, each failure occurs in no more than 10% of sessions for both models. Table 10 lists all counts and onset times. Thus, without retraining, IAP+DRP substantially reduces all three forms of collapse in both sliding-window models, in both controlled replay and adaptive interaction. Figure 8: LLM-judge scores over time. Mean Gemini-2.5-Flash ratings on FD-LHB-LLM for (a) coherence and (b) context to the partner’s preceding speech.

sections.heading: IAP+DRP also preserves response quality.
sections.text: Avoiding collapse does not guarantee the quality of what the model says. We therefore also score the content of each one-minute speaking bin on FD-LHB-LLM, using Gemini-2.5-Flash as a judge ( Fig. 8 ). It rates two aspects on a 1–5 scale: Coherence , whether the model’s speech is fluent and makes sense, and Context , whether it responds appropriately to what the partner said. Silent bins receive a score of 1. Both baselines fall to the lowest score within about ten minutes, whereas IAP+DRP keeps both scores steady for the full session. Sec. D.2 reports the same scores for FD-LHB-CANDOR, and Sec. D.4 for the ablation. Thus, IAP+DRP avoids collapse while keeping the model’s speech coherent and responsive.

sections.heading: 6.3 Ablation
sections.text: To investigate the effect of each component, we apply IAP and DRP separately and together to Moshi on the FD-LHB-CANDOR replays ( Fig. 9 ). For repetition in Fig. 9 a, DRP keeps every run repetition-free, and IAP also raises the repetition-free share from 35% to 90%, suggesting that initialization-anchor eviction contributes to repetition in part. For silence in Fig. 9 b, IAP raises the silence-free share from 0% to 67.5%, and adding DRP raises it further to 92.5%. For gibberish in Fig. 9 c, IAP alone keeps every run free of Gemini-defined gibberish, whereas DRP alone does not help, supporting the link between gibberish and initialization-anchor eviction. Thus, the two components are complementary: IAP addresses gibberish and most silence, DRP addresses repetition, and only their combination suppresses all three failures. Figure 9: Ablation of cache retention and repetition control. Curves show the proportion remaining free of (a) repetition, (b) prolonged silence, and (c) gibberish. Endpoint labels identify Baseline (B), IAP (I), DRP (D), and IAP+DRP (I+D).

We therefore measure the cost of IAP and DRP ( Table 1 ). The table reports two numbers for PersonaPlex: how many of 40 runs stay free of gibberish, and the real-time factor (RTF). RTF is the time, in seconds, needed to process one second of audio. An RTF below one means the model runs faster than real time. We measure RTF five times on an RTX A6000. We compare three methods. Baseline uses the standard FIFO cache. StreamingLLM-style ( Xiao et al., 2024b ) keeps the first four entries and re-indexes all remaining entries at every step. It avoids gibberish in every run, but its RTF is 1.03, so it cannot keep up in real time. Ours also avoids gibberish in every run, but reaches an RTF of 0.75, because IAP re-indexes only the first entry. In short, both methods prevent gibberish, but IAP is faster because it updates one entry per step instead of all of them. Sec. D.9 reports the cost of each component.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced FD-LHB to evaluate whether full-duplex speech models can sustain long conversations, using controlled replay and adaptive interaction. Across five models, sustained operation was limited by behavioral degradation or context exhaustion. Controlled experiments link silence and gibberish to Initialization-Anchor Eviction, and repetition to self-reinforcement from recent outputs. Guided by these findings, we applied two simple interventions: IAP retains the initialization anchor, while DRP discourages repetition and guards against prolonged silence. In replays of up to an hour, their combination reduces repetition, silence, and gibberish, and it also improves stability in adaptive conversations with an LLM partner. These gains validate our diagnosis. Both methods require neither retraining nor additional memory, and they run in real time. Overall, we identify how and why full-duplex models collapse in long conversations and show that simple, cause-specific fixes can prevent much of this collapse.

sections.heading: AI use statement

We used OpenAI Codex to assist with code development, debugging, and running analysis scripts. We used Anthropic Claude and OpenAI Codex to help draft and revise parts of the manuscript and to help find related work. sections.heading: Ethics Statement
sections.text: Our listening studies ( Secs. A.3 and D.8 ) were minimal-risk perceptual evaluations. Participants were adult, English-proficient crowdworkers recruited through Prolific, who provided informed consent before participating and could withdraw at any time. They listened to short clips of model-generated speech and answered forced-choice questions; no personally identifying information was collected beyond Prolific’s anonymized IDs. Participants were compensated at £9.00/hour, in line with Prolific’s recommended rate. The benchmark uses the CANDOR corpus, whose participants consented to recording and research use at collection time ( Reece et al., 2023 ) ; we access it under its research-access terms and release only a manifest of conversation IDs and crop boundaries, not the audio.

sections.heading: Replay input.
sections.text: As described in Sec. 3.1 , we remove the first three turns of each CANDOR conversation, keep the 40 longest, and use the speaker channel with more speech as input. Every model and condition receives exactly the same 16-kHz mono audio for a given conversation.

sections.heading: Interactive partner.
sections.text: The partner uses Gemini 2.5 Flash ( Comanici et al., 2025 ) for text and a facebook/mms-tts-eng VITS model ( Pratap et al., 2023 ) for 16-kHz speech. It sees the last 16 turns and replies in one or two casual sentences (temperature 0.9), asking natural follow-up questions and reacting naturally when the model’s speech is unclear or repetitive. Each session opens with one of ten everyday topics: hobbies, pets, food, travel, entertainment, work, music, family, exercise, or reading. Each model has 40 sessions, each lasting up to 20 minutes or until the model reaches its context limit. The complete partner prompt is given in Sec. A.7 .

Your name is Alex.” Moshi receives no text persona. For each model, Baseline and Ours use the same prompt, input, and sampling settings, so the two differ only in IAP and DRP. Full settings are listed in Table 9 .

sections.heading: Silence.
sections.text: We split each run into one-minute bins and call a bin silence if it contains fewer than three words. Prolonged-silence onset is the first of two consecutive silence bins, so brief pauses are not counted.

sections.heading: Gibberish.
sections.text: We measure gibberish in two ways. For benchmark results, Gemini-2.5-Flash (temperature 0) labels each one-minute bin with at least three words as gibberish or not. This label uses only the output text, so it applies to every model. For the mechanism analyses ( Appendix B ), we also use the model’s predictive entropy H t = − ∑ i p t ( i ) log p t ( i ) H_{t}=-\sum_{i}p_{t}(i)\log p_{t}(i) , where p t p_{t} is its distribution over the next text token at frame t t . High entropy means the model is uncertain about what to say next. Because it requires the model’s logits, which not every evaluated model exposes, we do not use it for benchmark results. A bin is labeled gibberish if its text is largely uninterpretable English, such as word salad, broken token fragments, or severely malformed syntax. Repetition, disfluency, generic or off-topic replies, and factual errors do not count as gibberish on their own. Gibberish onset is the first bin labeled gibberish. The exact classification prompt is given in Sec. A.7 .

sections.heading: Coherence and Context.
sections.text: Two further Gemini calls score each speaking bin from 1 to 5. Coherence rates whether the speech is fluent and makes sense; Context rates whether it responds appropriately to the partner, so this call also sees the partner’s recent speech. Silence bins receive a score of 1, so silence lowers the average instead of dropping out of it. The two scoring prompts are given in Sec. A.7 .

sections.heading: Aggregation.
sections.text: Tables 10 and 12 report how many runs reach each failure and, among those runs, the mean ± {}\pm{} SD onset time. Time-to-event curves( Figs. 7 and 9 ) show the fraction of runs that have not yet failed, estimated with the Kaplan–Meier method ( Kaplan and Meier, 1958 ) . Some runs end early because the model reaches its context limit or the input audio ends. Such a run is right-censored : we cannot know whether it would have failed later, so it counts as failure-free while it is running and is left out of the calculation after it ends. As a result, a curve’s final value can differ slightly from the raw fraction of failure-free runs in the tables. NR (not reached) means the event did not occur before the run ended.

sections.heading: A.3 Human Validation of the Gemini Gibberish Judge
sections.text: We checked the Gemini gibberish label against human listeners. Ten proficient-English listeners were recruited through Prolific, gave informed consent, and were paid for their time; two failed an attention check and were excluded, leaving eight. Each rated 40 one-minute clips from Moshi and PersonaPlex, half labeled gibberish by Gemini and half not. Listeners did not see the model, condition, transcript, or Gemini label. A clip is gibberish for humans if at least five of eight listeners say so. Gemini agrees with the human majority on 36 of 40 clips (Cohen’s κ = 0.80 \kappa=0.80 ; 1 means perfect agreement), similar to agreement between listeners (mean pairwise κ = 0.76 \kappa=0.76 ). In all four disagreements, humans heard gibberish that Gemini missed; Gemini never called normal speech gibberish. So the real amount of gibberish may be slightly higher than we report ( Table 4 ). sections.text: Our collapse metrics use the model’s text output, because every model produces text and this makes the metrics easy to reproduce. Here we check, on saved audio, that silence and repetition can also be heard in the speech ( Table 5 ). Gibberish is already checked by human listeners in Sec. A.3 . sections.heading: Silence.
sections.text: We split each one-minute bin into 20-ms frames and count a frame as active if it is louder than − 45 -45 dBFS, a level close to silence. A bin counts as silent if its share of active frames is below a cutoff. We use half of the runs to choose this cutoff and the other half to test it. We then check whether these silent bins match the bins that our word-count definition calls silent. The two definitions agree closely. They label almost the same minutes as silent (AUROC 0.983). Their silence onsets differ by only 0.67 minutes on average. Both definitions also find the same runs with prolonged silence.

sections.heading: Repetition.
sections.text: The model’s text output may not exactly match what it says aloud, so we also measure repetition from the audio. We transcribe all 160 replay runs of Moshi and PersonaPlex (Baseline and IAP+DRP) with two ASR models, Whisper small.en and large-v3 ( Radford et al., 2022 ) , and apply the same repetition criterion to each transcript ( Table 6 ). When the text shows repetition, the audio almost always does too (precision 1.00 with small.en and 0.98 with large-v3 ). The text-based metric also misses some audible repetition: about 30% of the runs flagged from audio are not flagged from text (recall 0.72 and 0.68), so it tends to undercount repetition. Even when repetition is measured from the audio, IAP+DRP still greatly reduces it compared with the baselines. Table 6: Repetition detected from text and from audio. sections.heading: A.5 Why Predictive Entropy Instead of Perplexity
sections.text: A common way to score generated speech is the perplexity (PPL) of its transcript under an external language model ( Lakhotia et al., 2021 ) , and full-duplex models, including Moshi, have been evaluated this way ( Défossez et al., 2024 ; Veluri et al., 2024 ) . However, PPL measures how predictable text is, not whether it makes sense. A repetitive loop is highly predictable and gets low PPL ( Holtzman et al., 2019 ; Park et al., 2024 ) , while unusual but readable speech can get high PPL. Table 7 shows examples where readable speech gets higher PPL than gibberish under three external LMs: GPT-2-large ( Radford et al., 2019 ) , Llama-3.1-8B ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) , and Mistral-7B-v0.3 ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) . Fig. 10 shows this over 2,750 speaking bins. Each point is one bin, placed by its PPL (x-axis) and its predictive entropy (y-axis). Along the x-axis, gibberish (red) and non-gibberish (green) bins cover overlapping PPL ranges, so no single PPL cutoff separates them. Some gibberish bins even get lower PPL than typical readable speech, as the two marked examples from Table 7 show. Along the y-axis, the two groups barely overlap: non-gibberish bins stay near zero entropy, while most gibberish bins lie far above. The same pattern holds for all three external LMs. We therefore use the Gemini label for benchmark results and predictive entropy for mechanism analyses. sections.heading: Gibberish.
sections.text: Unlike repetition and silence, gibberish onset requires only a single bin labeled gibberish. To check whether this choice matters, we also apply a stricter rule that requires three consecutive speaking bins labeled gibberish. For the two sliding-window models, the comparison between the baseline and IAP+DRP is unchanged. In replay, both baselines still reach gibberish in 40 of 40 runs and IAP+DRP in none. In interaction, the baselines drop only slightly (Moshi from 40 to 38 runs, PersonaPlex from 39 to 35), while IAP+DRP goes from 2 to 1 run for Moshi and stays at 0 for PersonaPlex. The stricter rule matters for the growing-context models. BayLing-Duplex often falls silent right after its first gibberish bin, so its count drops from 36 to 3 runs in replay and from 40 to 11 in interaction; its collapse then shows up as silence instead. Lychee-FD never produces three gibberish bins in a row, so its count drops to 0 in both tracks. A three-bin rule would therefore hide most gibberish in these models, and we use the single-bin rule.

sections.heading: FD-LHB-LLM partner.
sections.text: The system instruction is: You are a warm, friendly person on a casual phone call with a friend named Alex. Talk naturally about everyday life -- your day, hobbies, food, weekend plans, whatever comes up. React genuinely to what Alex says, ask follow-up questions, share your own little stories. Keep each turn SHORT (1-2 sentences), like real speech. Do NOT quiz them or recite facts -- just a nice flowing chat. If Alex says something odd, unclear, or repetitive, react like a real person would (e.g. ’wait, what?’, ’you okay?’, gently change topic). This particular call naturally revolves around {topic}. For the first turn, before any dialogue history is available, the user message is: (start the call with a warm, natural greeting, then soon bring up {topic})

sections.heading: A.8 Reproducibility
sections.text: FD-LHB involves no training: it runs existing models on fixed inputs and scores their outputs. Upon publication, we will release the code to run each model with IAP and DRP, the FD-LHB-LLM partner, and the metric computation, including the Gemini judge prompts. We will also release a manifest listing the CANDOR conversations and crop boundaries used in each experiment. CANDOR audio is available only through its research-access process, so we release the manifest rather than the audio. To reproduce the results, one rebuilds the inputs from the manifest, runs each model with the settings in Table 9 , and scores the outputs as described in Sec. A.2 .

sections.text: This section gives the setup of the diagnostic experiments in the main text and additional analyses of the two mechanisms: initialization-anchor eviction ( Sec. B.1 ) and self-reinforcing repetition ( Sec. B.2 ). The anchor analyses measure gibberish with predictive entropy ( Sec. A.2 ) and a threshold of H = 2 H=2 nats, rather than with the Gemini label.

sections.heading: B.1 Initialization-Anchor Eviction
sections.text: Figure 11: Late-conversation entropy when keeping different cache entries. (a) Keeping one early entry. (b) Keeping the first P P entries. Each dot is one run; the dashed line is H = 2 H=2 .

sections.heading: Evidence for the training premise.
sections.text: The main text assumes that every training sequence starts from an empty cache. We confirmed this in the official Moshi fine-tuning code ( Kyutai, 2025 ) , where each training sample is a segment of at most duration_sec seconds processed from an empty cache. Its README also warns that lowering duration_sec may cause the model to become silent more quickly at inference, which is consistent with a mismatch between training and inference lengths. This code covers fine-tuning rather than pretraining, and PersonaPlex is trained separately, so we test the role of anchor eviction directly with the interventions below.

sections.heading: Only the first entry matters.
sections.text: In the main text, we test which cache entries must be kept to prevent gibberish ( Fig. 5 ). Here we describe these tests in more detail and show the entropy of every run. Both tests use 15 CANDOR conversations for each of Moshi and PersonaPlex (30 runs per condition, fixed decoding seed). The identity test keeps one early entry and varies only which one it is, with its cache slot and position index fixed; the count test keeps the first P P entries, P ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 , 4 , … , 128 } P\in\{0,1,2,4,\dots,128\} . Fig. 11 shows each run’s entropy averaged over the late part of the conversation (minutes 13–20 in (a) and 10–30 in (b)), together with the mean and SD of each condition. In the identity test (a), only the first entry keeps every run below H = 2 H=2 ; every other choice leaves some runs far above it, so the result does not depend on the exact threshold. In the count test (b), entropy is high without any retained entry ( P = 0 P=0 ) and low for every P ≥ 1 P\geq 1 . Varying the decoding seed (42–46) on one PersonaPlex replay gives the same result. Figure 12: Position indices do not matter; the cache history does. (a) Output entropy over a conversation with the original, shifted, or re-indexed position indices. (b) Output entropy for the same 90-second audio, played after a fresh start or after a long conversation. Mean ± {}\pm{} SD over five seeds, pooled across Moshi and PersonaPlex.

sections.heading: Large position indices are not the cause.
sections.text: In long conversations, position indices grow far beyond those seen in training. Because RoPE depends only on relative distance, this should not matter, and Fig. 12 a confirms it. Shifting all positions by 10 5 10^{5} , or re-indexing the visible cache at every step so that its positions always run from 0 0 to L − 1 L-1 and never exceed the training range, leaves the onset of high entropy unchanged ( 12.1 ± 1.1 12.1\pm 1.1 minutes). Figure 13: The pinned anchor acts as an attention sink. Share of attention on the pinned anchor in one PersonaPlex replay with IAP ( P = 1 P=1 ), in 30-second averages. Dashed lines mark each full turnover of the sliding window.

sections.heading: The cache history is what matters.
sections.text: If position indices are not the cause, what differs between early and late in a conversation is the history stored in the cache. To isolate it, we play the same 90-second audio to the model twice: once right after a fresh start, with an empty cache, and once after the model has already run a long conversation. Everything else is identical, including the audio, the position indices, and the decoding settings. After a fresh start, entropy stays low ( H = 0.28 ± 0.04 H=0.28\pm 0.04 ); after the long conversation, it is very high ( H = 7.76 ± 0.35 H=7.76\pm 0.35 ; Fig. 12 b). The history in the cache therefore changes the model’s behavior.

sections.heading: The pinned anchor acts as an attention sink.
sections.text: IAP resembles StreamingLLM ( Xiao et al., 2024b ) , which also keeps the first few tokens of a sequence in the cache. StreamingLLM showed that language models place a large share of their attention on these first tokens, which it calls attention sinks , and that the model fails once they are removed. To check whether the pinned anchor plays the same role, we measure how much attention it receives over time. We run IAP ( P = 1 P=1 ) on one 14-minute PersonaPlex replay and record the share of attention that goes to the pinned anchor, averaged over all layers and heads ( Fig. 13 ). The anchor already receives about 32% of the attention during the first window. After the first window turnover at 4 minutes, its share rises above 60% and stays there. The pinned anchor therefore acts as an attention sink, and the model relies on it even more once the rest of the early context has left the window.

sections.heading: Word-insertion experiment.
sections.text: This section gives the setup of the word-insertion experiment in Sec. 4.2 ( Fig. 6 c). For each model, we take 20 CANDOR contexts that later reach repetition and branch them at least 30 seconds before repetition onset. Each branch receives d ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } d\in\{0,1,2,4,8,16,32\} forced occurrences of purple , a word absent from the preceding two minutes, and then runs freely for 20 seconds with three sampling seeds. We then measure how often purple appears among the model’s words in these 20 seconds. Forced occurrences are not counted. Without insertion, neither model says purple . In PersonaPlex, its share rises sharply up to d = 4 d=4 and keeps growing, reaching 28.4% at d = 32 d=32 . In Moshi, it stays below 10% at every dose.

sections.heading: Appendix C Implementation Details of IAP and DRP
sections.text: This section provides the implementation details and final settings of IAP and DRP. Evaluation results and ablations are reported in Appendix D .

sections.heading: C.1 Initialization-Anchor Pinning
sections.text: IAP pins the first KV entry ( P = 1 P=1 ) in the cache. The other L − 1 L-1 slots follow the normal FIFO update, so the cache size stays at L L and no training is needed. The pinned entry needs one extra step. RoPE ( Su et al., 2023 ) attention depends on the distance between query and key positions. If the pinned entry stayed at its original position, its distance to new queries would keep growing and soon exceed the distances seen in training. IAP therefore increases the pinned entry’s position by one each time the window slides, so that it always sits right before the oldest remaining entry. All other entries keep their positions, and each new entry receives the next position. To do this, we store the pinned key without RoPE applied and re-apply RoPE at its new position whenever it moves. Only this one key is updated at each step, instead of re-indexing the whole cache as in StreamingLLM ( Xiao et al., 2024b ) .

sections.heading: C.2 Duplex Repetition Penalty
sections.text: DRP modifies the text logits in two parts. The first penalizes recently used lexical tokens while keeping the total lexical probability unchanged, so that the penalty does not make the model less likely to speak. The second applies a small PAD correction after unusually long silent periods. DRP is applied before temperature scaling and top- k k filtering. When predictive entropy is used for analysis, it is computed from the original logits before applying DRP.

sections.text: DRP has two parts ( Sec. C.2 ). The first penalizes recent words ( eq. 1 ) and then adds an offset that keeps the total probability of words unchanged ( eq. 2 ). The second is a PAD safeguard against long silence ( eq. 3 ). To see what each part does, we compare them on 40 matched 20-minute PersonaPlex replays. All runs use IAP ( P = 1 P=1 ). sections.heading: D.8 Human Listening Comparison
sections.text: Because DRP penalizes every recently used word, including words that people naturally repeat, such as function words, backchannels, and topic words, it could make speech less natural. We ran a blinded A/B listening study to check whether DRP makes ordinary speech worse as a conversation goes on. We compare IAP+DRP with IAP alone on Moshi, isolating the effect of DRP. We keep IAP in both conditions because without it, both would produce gibberish after about 13 minutes, leaving nothing meaningful to compare in later phases. The study uses 37 matched pairs sampled early, middle, and late in the conversation (near 2, 10, and 18 minutes). In each trial, listeners heard 8 seconds of shared conversation context followed by two 12-second continuations, and chose A, B, or a tie on five dimensions: naturalness, intelligibility, prosody, conversational style, and appropriateness to the context. Conditions, transcripts, and generation times were hidden. Fifteen participants recruited through Prolific, who gave informed consent and were compensated, completed the study. We report a preference score for IAP+DRP: choosing it counts as 1, a tie as 0.5, and choosing IAP alone as 0, so 0.5 means no preference. Overall, scores are close to 0.5 on every dimension (0.47–0.53; Table 16 ), but the point estimates shift over time. Early in the conversation, they favor IAP alone (0.31–0.43), clearly so for intelligibility and context. In the middle phase, they favor IAP+DRP (0.56–0.60), clearly so for naturalness. In the late phase, they still lean toward IAP+DRP (0.53–0.60), but every interval includes 0.5. This suggests that DRP suppresses some natural word reuse early in a conversation but may help once repetition starts to build up. sections.text: DRP adds almost no cost (+2.7%), since it only edits the text logits. IAP adds 24.0%, but IAP+DRP still runs well within real time (RTF 0.75). sections.heading: Scope of the diagnosis.
sections.text: Our diagnosis covers only the two sliding-window models, Moshi and PersonaPlex. Growing-context models such as BayLing-Duplex also collapse before reaching their context limit, but we do not identify the cause, and IAP does not apply to them because they never evict cache entries. Even for the sliding-window models, our evidence for Initialization-Anchor Eviction comes mainly from controlled experiments. The fixed-slot test ( Sec. 4.1.2 ) shows that the first KV entry is important, while the matched-cache test ( Sec. B.1 ) shows that the previous cache state affects the failure. The fixed-slot test measures predictive entropy, so it does not directly measure dialogue quality. It also does not show how often the same failure occurs across different conversations or inputs. Broader tests across models, checkpoints, inputs, random seeds, architectures, and languages are needed.

sections.heading: Evaluation horizon and cross-model comparison.
sections.text: FD-LHB observes each model for a finite time, so NR means only that a failure did not occur before the run ended, not that the model would remain stable indefinitely. The evaluated models also differ in architecture, context management, and generation settings, including model-specific text temperatures in the adaptive track. Therefore, comparisons between methods within the same model are more directly interpretable than comparisons across different models.

sections.heading: Metrics and trade-offs.
sections.text: Our evaluation metrics are not perfect measures of overall conversation quality. First, our criteria ( Sec. 3.2 ) detect repetition, silence, and gibberish separately. A conversation that avoids these failures may still be incoherent or irrelevant. Second, reducing one type of failure can introduce a trade-off elsewhere. For example, DRP may penalize natural word reuse, and listeners preferred IAP alone over IAP+DRP early in the conversation ( Sec. D.8 ). Moreover, the proposed methods do not eliminate all failures: in PersonaPlex, IAP+DRP still produces a two-minute silence in 19 of 40 replays. Finally, the Gemini-based gibberish detector is also imperfect. Our human validation ( Sec. A.3 ) found no false positives but did find some missed cases, suggesting that the reported gibberish rates may underestimate the true frequency. These limitations motivate broader and longer-term human evaluation of both conversation quality and possible trade-offs.

Affiliation: Kyung Hee University, South Korea Abstract Full-duplex speech models listen and speak at the same time, which makes them promising for natural, open-ended conversation. But can they sustain a coherent conversation for tens of minutes? Because they generate a token every frame, even while listening, they exhaust their context windows within minutes. Yet existing benchmarks evaluate only single turns or a few conversational rounds, too short to expose the long-horizon problem. We introduce the Full-Duplex Long-Horizon Benchmark (FD-LHB), which tests five recent full-duplex models on long replayed conversations and in live conversation with an LLM partner. Every evaluated model eventually either degrades or exhausts its context. Models that keep the full history often degrade before their context runs out, while sliding-window models still fall into repetition , silence , and gibberish . For sliding-window models, we identify two contributing mechanisms. Gibberish and silence are linked to Initialization-Anchor Eviction, where the sliding window discards the first KV entry. Repetition is also reinforced by the model’s own recent outputs. Guided by this diagnosis, we apply two simple fixes: Initialization-Anchor Pinning (IAP) keeps that first entry, and Duplex Repetition Penalty (DRP) discourages echoing while guarding against prolonged silence. Together, they support the diagnosis and, without retraining, substantially reduce conversational collapse in replays of up to an hour while running in real time. 1 Introduction 0 min — coherent “Hi, my name’s Alex. I’m in the Seattle area. Where are you?” 6 min — repetition “… you go back to your normal life , you go back to your normal life , and then you go back to your normal life …” 9–10 min — silence (no lexical output) 13 min — gibberish “core offensive of the core the good blue of the event seven…” Figure 1: Example of long-conversation collapse. It shows progression of coherent speech, repetition, silence, and gibberish, with timestamps aligned to the timeline in Figure 2a. Human conversation can continue for tens of minutes or longer, as speakers move between long turns, silence, interruptions, backchannels (e.g., “uh-huh” or “yeah”), and overlapping speech ( Levinson and Torreira, 2015 ) . Full-duplex speech models ( Défossez et al., 2024 ; Roy et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) aim to support this form of interaction by listening and speaking concurrently. Maintaining this behavior over long conversations remains difficult because, unlike text LLMs or half-duplex systems, full-duplex models continuously generate tokens frame by frame, even while listening. This rapidly fills the context with silence and recurring backchannels, while each generated output also becomes part of the next input and can influence later generation. Despite these challenges, long-horizon behavior in full-duplex models remains poorly understood. Existing full-duplex benchmarks ( Lin et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2026b ; Lin et al., 2026a ; Peng et al., 2025 ; Arora et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2026 ) evaluate capabilities such as turn-taking, interruption handling, pauses, backchanneling, and overlapping speech, within a single turn or a few conversational rounds, not over many minutes. Existing models manage conversation history in one of two ways. Growing-context models ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) keep the full interaction, so their context grows until it reaches a context limit. Sliding-window models ( Défossez et al., 2024 ; Roy et al., 2026 ) keep only the most recent frames, discarding the oldest as new ones arrive, so they can run indefinitely with fixed-size cache. Whether either design is sufficient for long-form full-duplex interaction, and how the models fail when it is not, has not been systematically investigated. The growing-context model (c) BayLing-Duplex develops gibberish and silence before reaching its context limit. To investigate this problem, we introduce the Full-Duplex Long-Horizon Benchmark (FD-LHB) , a benchmark designed specifically to evaluate full-duplex models over extended interaction. FD-LHB combines controlled replay of CANDOR conversations ( Reece et al., 2023 ) with adaptive interaction against an LLM-based spoken partner. Using FD-LHB, we find that every evaluated model eventually either degrades, through repetition, silence, or gibberish ( Fig. 1 ), or exhausts its context: sliding-window models collapse even though their memory never runs out ( Fig. 2 a,b), and growing-context models can collapse before reaching their context limit ( Fig. 2 c). We then ask why these collapses occur, focusing on the two sliding-window models, and identify two contributing mechanisms ( Sec. 4 ). Silence and gibberish are linked to Initialization-Anchor Eviction : the sliding window eventually discards the first KV entry computed without prior cached context. We hypothesize that this dependence reflects a mismatch between empty-cache training and continual inference. We also identify Self-Reinforcing Repetition : a word the model has recently said becomes more likely to be said again. Finally, these mechanisms motivate two simple fixes that need no retraining. Initialization-Anchor Pinning (IAP) keeps the first KV entry in the cache while the rest of the window slides as usual, and Duplex Repetition Penalty (DRP) discourages recently used words without making the model less likely to speak. Together, they substantially reduce repetition, silence, and gibberish in both sliding-window models. In addition, the combined method still runs in real time and is faster than a StreamingLLM-style baseline ( Xiao et al., 2024b ) while matching its cache stability. We do not claim that they solve long-horizon full-duplex modeling; rather, our results show that simple fixes targeting the two identified causes prevent much of the collapse. Our contributions are as follows: • FD-LHB: benchmark for long-horizon full-duplex interaction. FD-LHB measures when and how conversational failures emerge through two tracks: 40 controlled replays evaluated up to 60 minutes (FD-LHB-CANDOR) and 40 adaptive sessions up to 20 minutes (FD-LHB-LLM). • Systematic characterization and diagnosis of collapse. Across five recent full-duplex models using sliding-window or growing-context, we characterize the onset and progression of three failure modes: repetition, prolonged silence, and gibberish. Experiments on two sliding-window models identify Initialization-Anchor Eviction and Self-Reinforcing Repetition as mechanisms underlying the collapse. • Validation through training-free interventions. Simple, targeted fixes reduce gibberish from 100% to 0%. Repetition falls from 65% to 0% in Moshi and 90% to 2.5% in PersonaPlex; prolonged silence falls from 100% to 7.5% and 85% to 47.5%, respectively. These interventions require no retraining and can be incorporated into compatible baselines at inference time. 2 Related Work 2.1 Full-Duplex Speech Generation and Streaming Interaction Models such as Moshi ( Défossez et al., 2024 ) , PersonaPlex ( Roy et al., 2026 ) , Raon-SpeechChat ( Kim et al., 2026 ) , BayLing-Duplex ( Fang et al., 2026 ) , and Lychee-FD ( Liu et al., 2026 ) support low-latency full-duplex interaction. Existing benchmarks ( Lin et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2026b ; Lin et al., 2026a ; Peng et al., 2025 ; Arora et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Ray et al., 2026 ) evaluate turn-taking, overlap, interruption handling, multi-round quality, and task completion, but do not examine their stability over extended conversations. We address this gap by evaluating repetition, silence, and gibberish during continuous generation lasting tens of minutes. 2.2 Long-Horizon Stability and KV-Cache Management Autoregressive generation can suffer from degeneration in text ( Holtzman et al., 2019 ) , video ( Ge et al., 2022 ) , and speech ( Song et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) . Scheduled Sampling ( Bengio et al., 2015 ) and Professor Forcing ( Lamb et al., 2016 ) address the mismatch between training and generation through modified training procedures. We instead investigate instability during continual full-duplex inference, where generated outputs can reinforce later repetition ( Xu et al., 2022 ; Zhu et al., 2023 ) . DRP targets this feedback by modifying token selection without retraining. Beyond repetition, continual inference raises the question of how conversation history should be retained. Under a fixed memory budget, StreamingLLM ( Xiao et al., 2024b ) preserves initial attention sinks together with recent tokens, as do LM-Infinite ( Han et al., 2024 ) and InfLLM ( Xiao et al., 2024a ) ; H2O ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) retains tokens with high accumulated attention; and SnapKV ( Li et al., 2024 ) selects prompt positions using attention patterns from an observation window. Building on these studies, we examine the role of the first KV entry in the long-horizon stability of full-duplex speech models. StreamingLLM is the closest to IAP because it also preserves entries from the beginning of the sequence. In Moshi and PersonaPlex, the first KV entry alone prevents gibberish in all tested runs, whereas the tested later entries do not do so consistently ( Sec. 4.1.2 ). We hypothesize that this dependence reflects initialization-anchor eviction: training chunks always begin with this entry, but long inference evicts it ( Sec. 4.1 ). IAP keeps only this entry and updates only its position index, which is cheaper than re-indexing the whole cache as StreamingLLM does ( Sec. 6.4 ). 3 Full-Duplex Long-Horizon Benchmark 3.1 Evaluation Protocol Existing benchmarks do not test whether these models remain stable over sustained interactions lasting tens of minutes. To address this gap, we introduce the Full-Duplex Long-Horizon Benchmark (FD-LHB). FD-LHB has two complementary tracks: controlled replay ( FD-LHB-CANDOR ) and adaptive interaction ( FD-LHB-LLM ). Replay (FD-LHB-CANDOR) gives every model the same recorded human speech, enabling controlled comparison, but it is non-interactive: the input doesn’t respond to the model’s output. Adaptive (FD-LHB-LLM), by contrast, is interactive, with an LLM partner whose synthesized speech reacts to the model’s behavior like a real conversation, but this means the input differs across runs, making controlled comparison harder. Because each track compensates for the other’s weakness, the two are complementary. FD-LHB-CANDOR. FD-LHB-CANDOR is built from CANDOR ( Reece et al., 2023 ) , a corpus of long, natural human conversations. We remove the first three turns from each conversation to exclude greetings and initial silence, rank the conversations by their remaining duration, and select the longest 40. The resulting streams have minimum, mean, and maximum durations of 55.5, 67.4, and 92.6 minutes, respectively. We evaluate each replay for up to 60 minutes, or until the available conversation ends. For each conversation, we select the speaker channel containing more speech and use it as the fixed audio input to the evaluated model. Thus, although the original CANDOR recordings are interactive human conversations, FD-LHB-CANDOR replays the same fixed input to every model, enabling controlled comparison. FD-LHB-LLM. To complement the non-interactive fixed replay of FD-LHB-CANDOR, FD-LHB-LLM evaluates the model in a closed-loop conversation with an LLM-based spoken partner whose responses adapt to the evaluated model’s output. At each turn, Gemini-2.5-Flash ( Comanici et al., 2025 ) generates the partner’s next text response from the recent dialogue history, and a local facebook/mms-tts-eng VITS model ( Pratap et al., 2023 ) converts it to 16-kHz speech for the evaluated model. The evaluated model’s response is then returned to Gemini, which generates the next partner turn. Each session begins with one of ten everyday-life topics, such as hobbies, travel, family, or work, and the partner responds adaptively to the evaluated model rather than following a fixed script. We run 40 sessions per dialogue model, each for up to 20 minutes or until the model reaches its context capacity. 3.2 Failure Modes and Onset Metrics As shown in Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 , we observe three main forms of long-horizon collapse: repetition , silence , and gibberish . To measure when each form first appears, we define its onset time . Repetition is evaluated over 32-word windows, while silence and gibberish are evaluated in one-minute bins. For each form, the onset is the start of the first window or bin that meets its criterion. Repetition. We measure repetition with word-level Seq-Rep-4 ( Xu et al., 2022 ) , which captures repeated four-word patterns in the model’s recent output. We use this metric because it detects recurring phrase-level patterns. We compute it over 32-word windows and define a window as repetitive when Seq-Rep-4 ≥ 0.30 \geq 0.30 ; examples around this threshold are shown in Table 3 . The repetition onset is the start of the first of two consecutive repetitive windows, so a single repeated phrase is not counted. Silence. We measure silence using the number of spoken words in each bin. A bin is considered silent when it contains fewer than three words. To exclude short conversational pauses, we define prolonged-silence onset as the first bin of two consecutive silent bins. Gibberish. We characterize gibberish using two measures: a Gemini-2.5-Flash judge and predictive entropy, computed from the model’s distribution over its next text token. Gemini classifies each one-minute speaking bin as either gibberish or non-gibberish, while predictive entropy measures the model’s uncertainty. We evaluate bins containing at least three words and define the gibberish onset as the first bin classified as gibberish by Gemini. A blinded listening study with eight raters shows that the judge never calls normal speech gibberish but sometimes misses real gibberish ( Sec. Both models use a sliding window that discards the oldest cached entries as new ones arrive. As shown in Fig. 3 , training splits each sample into chunks that start from an empty cache, so every chunk begins with an initialization anchor : the first KV entry, computed without any earlier cached state. We confirmed this setup in the official Moshi fine-tuning code; whether pretraining and PersonaPlex training follow it is not public ( Sec. B.1 ). At inference, however, the cache is never reset. Once it is full, the oldest entries are evicted, starting with the initialization anchor. Training therefore always contains an anchor, whereas long inference eventually does not, creating a training–inference mismatch. In text generation, repeated content in the context makes the same content more likely, so a loop can reinforce itself ( Xu et al., 2022 ; Zhu et al., 2023 ) . Based on this, we hypothesize that recent outputs similarly reinforce repetition in full-duplex speech, and test this hypothesis in Fig. 6 . First, the most repeated words during repetition periods are short, frequent words such as of , then , and you , and backchannels such as yeah and okay ( Fig. 6 a). Second, for each PersonaPlex run we select the word that dominates during repetition periods and track how frequently it occurs. It starts rising before onset and keeps rising afterward ( Fig. 6 b). This suggests that a repetition loop does not appear suddenly, but grows from a word the model has already been saying. Third, we insert purple , a word absent from the previous context, and count how often the model repeats it over the next 20 s. Recurrence increases with more insertions in both models, most strongly in PersonaPlex ( Fig. 6 c). Together, these results show that recent exposure makes a word recur. 5 Testing the Diagnosis with Training-Free Interventions The diagnosis yields two testable predictions: retaining the initialization anchor should reduce failures associated with cache eviction, and limiting reinforcement from recent words should reduce repetition. We test these predictions with Initialization-Anchor Pinning (IAP) and Duplex Repetition Penalty (DRP), respectively. Both are training-free methods that operate at inference time and can be applied to existing models. 5.1 Initialization-Anchor Pinning (IAP) Sec. 4.1.2 showed that keeping the first KV entry is enough to prevent gibberish, while keeping more initial entries adds nothing. IAP therefore keeps this initialization anchor instead of letting the sliding window evict it. Until the cache is full, nothing changes. Once it is full, the model normally drops the oldest entry each time a new one arrives. IAP does the same, except that it never drops the anchor: when a new entry arrives, it removes the oldest entry after the anchor instead. This is done in every layer. As in StreamingLLM ( Xiao et al., 2024b ) , the anchor’s position index stays next to the rest of the window so that position indices remain continuous. StreamingLLM, however, re-indexes the entire cache as the window slides. IAP instead simply increases the anchor’s index by one each time the window slides. Only this single entry changes, which keeps IAP cheap ( Sec. 6.4 ). 5.2 Duplex Repetition Penalty (DRP) DRP reduces repeated words without letting the model fall silent instead. It changes only the assistant’s text-token logits; the audio streams are unchanged. DRP penalizes any word that appeared in the model’s last N = 512 N{=}512 lexical tokens, using the standard repetition penalty of CTRL ( Keskar et al., 2019 ) : a positive logit is divided by ρ \rho and a negative one is multiplied by it. A word is penalized based only on whether it appeared recently, not on how often. PAD and EPAD , which the model uses for listening and turn-taking ( Roy et al., 2026 ; Défossez et al., 2024 ) , are excluded from this penalty. Penalizing words lowers their total probability and makes PAD and EPAD relatively more likely. To undo this, we raise all word logits by the same amount, so that the total probability of words stays the same as before the penalty. This removes the relative boost that the penalty gives to PAD and EPAD. With this penalty alone, repetition decreases, but PAD can still dominate for long periods, leaving the model silent. To address this, when the model has been silent for a long time and the user is quiet, we gradually lower the PAD logit. We do not force any token; the model still samples its next token as usual ( Sec. D.9 reports the cost of each component. 7 Conclusion We introduced FD-LHB to evaluate whether full-duplex speech models can sustain long conversations, using controlled replay and adaptive interaction. Across five models, sustained operation was limited by behavioral degradation or context exhaustion. Controlled experiments link silence and gibberish to Initialization-Anchor Eviction, and repetition to self-reinforcement from recent outputs. Guided by these findings, we applied two simple interventions: IAP retains the initialization anchor, while DRP discourages repetition and guards against prolonged silence. In replays of up to an hour, their combination reduces repetition, silence, and gibberish, and it also improves stability in adaptive conversations with an LLM partner. These gains validate our diagnosis. Both methods require neither retraining nor additional memory, and they run in real time. Overall, we identify how and why full-duplex models collapse in long conversations and show that simple, cause-specific fixes can prevent much of this collapse.
